title: Common mistakes of new investors
subtitle: Pitfalls to avoid
openingQuestion: A friend texts: 'Take out another VND 200 million on margin, this ticker's a sure win, got a tip from a VIP group.' What is the biggest hidden mistake in this advice?
openingOptions: This advice is only wrong if the friend giving it has no prior stock-investing experience
There's nothing wrong here - using margin to scale up profit when you already have good information in hand is a reasonable decision
Combining leverage with a stock tip and dumping it all into one ticker
This advice is only wrong because the VND 200 million mentioned is too small a sum to make a meaningful difference
explanation: This is a classic combination of three mistakes at once: using leverage (margin) to amplify risk, trusting a rumor/tip with no analytical basis, and having no diversification (dumping it all into one ticker). Each factor alone is already risky, combined all three the risk multiplies many times over.

diagram.label: + Dumping it all into one ticker

realWorldExample.company: The wave of mass margin calls in 2022
realWorldExample.description: During the sharp market drop in Vietnam in 2022, many individual investors used margin to buy real-estate and securities stocks based on 'tips' from Zalo and Telegram groups. When prices fell sharply, securities firms were forced to force-sell to recover their loans, causing many investors to lose most or all of their capital - a clear demonstration of the consequences of combining leverage with poorly grounded decisions.

quiz.question: Why is 'dumping all your capital into one stock because you're sure it will rise' a common and dangerous mistake?
options: Because a single stock always has a lower listed price than a portfolio no matter how careful the original analysis was
Because if the forecast is wrong, all your capital is at risk instead of just a portion
Because each account is only allowed to hold one stock at most
Because the law bans concentrating capital in a single stock
quiz.explanation: No investment is ever 100% certain. Diversification (not putting all your eggs in one basket) helps minimize the damage if a specific investment goes wrong, no matter how carefully it was analyzed.

quiz.question: The mistake of 'trading too frequently' (overtrading) mainly causes harm for which reason?
options: Because the more you trade, the correspondingly higher your profit
Because the exchange hard-caps the number of orders allowed per day
Because fees and tax rise, and decisions turn emotional
Because trading frequency has no effect at all on results
quiz.explanation: Every trade incurs a fee and a 0.1% sale tax on the transaction value. The more you trade, the more accumulated cost, while buying and selling repeatedly based on short-term movement usually stems more from emotion than grounded analysis.

quiz.question: Why is 'having no clear plan/goal before buying' considered the root of many other mistakes?
options: Because the law requires a written plan before buying
Because without a plan you can't open a trading account
Because having a plan eliminates all risk of loss entirely
Because without clear criteria, it's easy to get swept up by rumors
quiz.explanation: A clear plan (goal, time horizon, buy/sell criteria, allocation levels) is the framework that helps an investor make consistent decisions. Without it, every decision easily gets swayed by momentary emotion or unverified information - the root cause of most of the other mistakes listed.

quiz.question: After buying a stock, an investor only reads analyses that support their decision and ignores dissenting opinions. What is this mistake called?
options: Confirmation bias: seeking evidence to defend an existing conclusion
The anchoring effect in valuation
Loss aversion when the portfolio falls
Survivorship bias when looking back at history, a pattern that repeats across many investors
quiz.explanation: Confirmation bias makes us gather evidence to defend an existing conclusion instead of testing it. The most practical way to fight it is to actively seek the opposing thesis: if you can't write three reasons this investment could be wrong, you don't understand it well enough yet.

quiz.question: Why is 'investing money you'll need in the next six months' a serious mistake even if you pick the right stock?
options: Because securities firms don't allow withdrawals within the first six months which is a scheduling problem, not a stock-picking one
Because the forced sale date driven by your cash need may not align with a good price
Because transfer tax on short-term holdings is many times higher
Because good stocks only start rising after at least a year of holding
quiz.explanation: Your time horizon determines which asset type fits. Money with a near-term spending schedule forces you to sell on a predetermined date, and that date could easily land right at the bottom of a downturn - turning a sound investment into a real loss.

keyTakeaways: Three of the most common mistakes for new investors: dumping all capital into one ticker, over-using leverage (margin), and trusting unverified 'tips'
Trading too frequently (overtrading) raises trading costs and usually stems from emotion rather than analysis
Having no clear investment plan from the start is the root cause of getting easily swept up by rumors and short-term volatility
Diversifying your portfolio and avoiding excessive leverage are the two most basic protective principles for beginners

practicePrompt.question: You just opened a securities account 1 month ago. In that month, you placed 40 different buy/sell orders based on rumors in a chat group, with no clear plan from the start, and are currently down 15%. What is the core mistake here?
options: No clear plan from the start - the root cause behind being swayed so easily by rumors
Simply bad luck in the first month, unrelated to how you made investment decisions
Because your initial capital was too small relative to what's needed to profit short-term
Because the stock market in general was operating inefficiently and abnormally during that period
practicePrompt.explanation: Having no clear plan is the root cause leading to other mistakes: trading too frequently, trusting tips, and making emotional decisions instead of disciplined ones.

application.title: Audit your own portfolio
application.message: Review your current portfolio (if you have one): are you overconcentrated in one ticker, using margin, or holding any position bought purely because of an unverified 'tip'?
application.secondary: Self-checking these three mistakes early helps you avoid learning a costly lesson later.

sections.text: Almost every seasoned investor, if honest, will admit to having made at least a few of the mistakes below when starting out. Knowing these traps in advance won't help you avoid them entirely, but it will certainly help reduce the damage significantly.
Mistake 1: Dumping all capital into one 'sure-win' ticker

No stock is a '100% sure win'. Even a good business can face unexpected setbacks: poor governance, an industry crisis, a policy change, or simply the market repricing its expectations. When you concentrate all your capital in one ticker, a single analytical mistake or an unexpected shock can wipe out most of your assets. This is why the principle of portfolio diversification is repeated over and over.
Mistake 2: Using leverage (margin) without understanding its risk

Margin lets you borrow from a securities firm to buy more stock, amplifying both gains and losses. The problem is when the market falls, your account can get 'margin called' (requiring you to add more money or be force-sold) right when the price is at its lowest - turning a temporary loss into a permanent one because it gets sold right at the bottom.

items: Dumping all capital into one stock, with no diversification
Using margin (leverage) without understanding the margin-call and force-sell mechanism
Buying based on 'tips' or rumors on social media instead of your own fundamental analysis
Trading too frequently (overtrading), raising fee-plus-tax costs and leading to emotional decisions
Having no goal, time horizon, and buy/sell criteria clearly set before putting money in
Ignoring costs and tax when calculating actual profit

sections.label: A subtler mistake: 'investing' out of familiarity
sections.text: Many beginners choose to buy a stock just because the company name feels familiar (for example buying a bank stock because they use that bank's services, or buying their own employer's stock) without actually analyzing financial statements, revenue growth, or valuation. Familiarity creates a false sense of safety - it doesn't substitute for fundamental analysis.

This is perhaps the root of most other mistakes. Without setting a goal in advance (long-term accumulation or short-term trading), a time horizon, risk tolerance, and specific criteria for buying more/selling/cutting losses, every investment decision becomes a whimsical reaction to market movement or rumors - exactly the ideal environment for greed and fear (covered in the previous lesson) to take control.

lines: Most new-investor mistakes don't come from a lack of analytical knowledge, but from a lack of discipline and a clear plan.
Diversifying, limiting leverage, analyzing yourself instead of trusting tips, and having a plan set in advance are the four most basic shields.
